title: India Has Mapped 197 Districts That Could Starve if the Monsoon Fails. The Government Has a Plan.
excerpt: Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan unveiled state-by-state contingency plans as Pacific temperatures crossed the El Niño threshold. Some scientists warn this could become the strongest El Niño ever recorded.
body:
# India Has Mapped 197 Districts That Could Starve if the Monsoon Fails. The Government Has a Plan.

India's Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said on Tuesday that the government has identified 197 districts across the country as most vulnerable to the impact of El Niño — and has drawn up state-by-state contingency plans to protect the kharif crop season that is just weeks away.

"The concern about El Niño is always on my mind 24x7," Chouhan told reporters in New Delhi. "Not definitive, but 197 districts are identified as most vulnerable. We have prepared a contingency plan for each state. We will leave no stone unturned to tackle this."

The announcement came as Pacific sea surface temperatures officially crossed the El Niño threshold for the first time this season. The Niño 3.4 index — the benchmark measurement of temperature anomalies in the central-to-eastern equatorial Pacific — reached +0.81°C for the week ending June 7, just above the +0.80°C trigger, according to Australia's Bureau of Meteorology. Every major forecasting model indicates the Pacific will continue warming through the second half of 2026.

Some climate scientists have begun calling it the "Godzilla El Niño." ClimateAi, a leading agricultural weather forecasting firm, has warned that sea surface temperatures could rise more than 2.5°C above normal by late 2026 — a level that would make this the strongest El Niño ever recorded, surpassing the devastating events of 1997 and 2015.

## The Monsoon Is Already Short

The southwest monsoon arrived on June 4, three days behind schedule, and its advance has been sluggish. As of this week, cumulative rainfall across India is 18 percent below the long-period average. The India Meteorological Department has downgraded its seasonal forecast to 90 percent of normal rainfall — a classification that formally qualifies as "below normal" and signals drought risk across rain-fed zones.

Maharashtra's state authorities have issued an advisory warning farmers not to begin sowing based on scattered pre-monsoon showers. "Current weather conditions do not indicate satisfactory and widespread rainfall across the state," the notice said. "Farmers should not undertake sowing operations merely on the basis of forecast thunderstorm activity." The state has urged farmers to delay planting until sustained, widespread precipitation is established — a wait that could push sowing weeks behind its normal window.

The monsoon delivers roughly 70 percent of India's annual rainfall and sustains more than half the country's farmland. In the last major El Niño — 2015-16 — India received just 86 percent of normal rainfall. Multiple states declared drought. Crop yields fell, food prices rose, and rural distress rippled into the broader economy for two consecutive years. This situation could also impact the Indian diaspora, as remittances from abroad often support families back home during such crises. A decline in agricultural output may lead to increased food prices, affecting the purchasing power of NRIs sending money back to their families.

## Seeds, Contingencies, and a National Campaign

Chouhan said the government has stockpiled seeds and essential agricultural inputs to ensure rapid response if conditions deteriorate further. A nationwide awareness drive, "Khet Bachao Abhiyan" — loosely translated as the "Save the Farm Campaign" — is being rolled out across the 197 identified districts to help farmers decide when and what to plant.

The vulnerable districts span India's most critical agricultural belts: central and eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, parts of Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra's rain-fed Marathwada and Vidarbha regions, and stretches of Rajasthan, Karnataka, and Telangana. These areas rely almost entirely on monsoon rainfall for their summer crop cycle. Without adequate precipitation between July and September, the kharif harvest — which includes rice, pulses, cotton, sugarcane, and oilseeds — faces serious risk.

The sugarcane sector is already under strain. India's planted area has stagnated even as the government recently cancelled its sugar export window, halting shipments at under 800,000 metric tons against a planned allocation of 1.6 million. Industry experts warn that a poor monsoon could thin carry-forward inventories to levels that force the government to prioritise domestic retail supply over ethanol blending and export commitments — a trade-off with implications for India's biofuel targets.

## One Possible Lifeline in the Indian Ocean

Not all forecasts point to catastrophe. Australia's Bureau of Meteorology has flagged the Indian Ocean Dipole — a separate climate pattern that can offset El Niño's drying effect on India — as a potential positive factor. A positive IOD pushes additional moisture toward the subcontinent, and in 1997, a strong positive IOD helped India avoid drought despite a raging Super El Niño in the Pacific.

In 2026, however, the IOD remains neutral, with an index value of -0.34°C as of June 7. Most models suggest it will stay neutral through at least July, with the possibility of a positive shift in August or September. Whether it materialises in time to rescue the monsoon's critical mid-season months is uncertain.

For a country where 60 percent of farmers still depend on rain to water their fields, the arithmetic is unforgiving. A weak monsoon hits the poorest first — the small and marginal farmers who grow food for their families before they grow it for the market. Their distress then travels up the chain: into wholesale mandis, through food processing plants, and eventually onto supermarket shelves in Mumbai, Delhi, and diaspora grocery stores from New Jersey to London. This interconnectedness emphasizes the importance of monitoring agricultural health, as it directly impacts food security for families both in India and abroad.

The government says it is prepared. The next eight weeks will determine whether its contingency plans are enough — or whether India faces an agricultural emergency that reverberates from village fields to global commodity markets.

*Sources: Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan (press conference, June 9), India Meteorological Department, Australia's Bureau of Meteorology, ClimateAi, The Hindu BusinessLine*
